sections.heading: Which uncertainty should you check first?

blocks.title: Prioritise What to Test First
blocks.subtitle: Planned 2½-minute explainer + worksheet demo
blocks.note: No playable video or generated media is attached.

scenes.title: Not every unknown comes first
scenes.narration: You have made assumptions visible. Now decide which uncertainty to investigate first. Prioritisation is a reasoned learning choice, not a success score. Start with claims that could change the next decision, while respecting dependencies and critical constraints.

scenes.title: Compare decision impact and uncertainty
scenes.narration: For each candidate, ask what would change if it were wrong and how much relevant evidence you have. High uncertainty means unresolved information. Do not invent numeric scores or treat confidence as proof. Preserve the evidence status and strongest competing explanation.

scenes.title: Check prerequisites
scenes.narration: Some checks depend on access, earlier learning or a clear group definition. A payment question may be premature when you do not know the buyer. Pending permission cannot be overridden by high impact. A permitted prerequisite check may need to come first.

scenes.title: Consider ethical access and effort
scenes.visual: Founder compares bounded tasks on a calendar.
scenes.narration: Choose a feasible method for the question, not just the easiest activity. Consider relevant participants, voluntary participation, privacy, time and resources. A cheap test that answers the wrong question is not useful. Keep a fallback if access fails.

scenes.title: Choose and explain the sequence
scenes.visual: Editable first, later and reconsider cards.
scenes.narration: Select a provisional first priority. Explain why it comes before other candidates, what you are deferring and the strongest reason against your choice. No automatic ranking is calculated. Record what new evidence or constraint would change the sequence.

scenes.title: Create your priority plan
scenes.narration: Build your Validation Priority Plan with three candidate assumptions or honestly labeled options still to find. Compare them, choose a first learning priority, note prerequisites and plan the next check. Selection is not evidence collected; the next lesson designs a small validation experiment.

sections.label: 02 / LEARN
sections.heading: Choose the next question that can change a decision.

children: Compare
decision impact
uncertainty
dependencies
ethical access
and
effort
. Impact is what changes if a claim is wrong. Uncertainty is the unresolved evidence gap. A dependency is a prerequisite.
Choose three specific candidate assumptions from your register.
Preserve evidence/status and consequence if wrong.
Identify prerequisites and constraints.
Choose a fitting, feasible learning check.
Explain the first priority, deferred checks and review trigger.
Illustrative example:

permission is pending for an observation. A permitted source/access check may come first. A high-impact assumption does not grant permission; asking about payment may be premature if the buyer role is unknown.

No total or automatic ranking is calculated. Unknowns are acceptable with a plan. Do not choose a test just because it is easy or supports your preferred idea. A negative result may justify refining or pausing.
Review assumption register
